title: Will AI Bots Ever Catch on for Online Shopping?
description:
"If you currently use an AI agent that signs in to your account with your credentials, it may no longer be able to connect," American Express told its customers today (according to Slashdot reader Smonster). And ahile Walmart's site welcomes AI agents, there's blocks or limitations on them from Amazon, eBay, Kohl's and United Airlines, CNBC reports. And other sites "have added provisions to their terms of service spelling out that they're not liable if users' AI-driven purchases go wrong..."

The hiccups threaten to stunt the growth of shopping agents by creating a clunky and frustrating experience for users who are just starting to experiment with the tools. The question of who takes the blame when a transaction goes wrong also remains unclear. 

Despite those challenges, analysts remain bullish about agentic commerce's potential. U.S. revenue from agentic commerce could reach up to $1 trillion by 2030, analysts at McKinsey and ICSC forecast in April. Retailers and tech companies are also positioning agents as a helping hand for holiday shopping. Walmart on Tuesday touted its partnership with Meta, saying consumers could "put an AI agent to work" to nab Black Friday deals.... 

For users hoping to turn their online shopping over to AI agents, the experience can be unpredictable. Agents encounter a patchwork of permissions across various websites. Retailers such as Coach and Gap allow AI bots to browse but not check out, while others such as Target sometimes "block shopping agents by accident," according to an audit conducted in August by agent security company Billions Network. Amazon has responded the most aggressively to agents by walling off its site entirely. The company rankled Elon Musk last month after it prevented his Grok Bot from placing orders. In September, the company also blocked Meta's Muse from shopping on its platform, saying it never agreed to participate in the program. And last November, Amazon sued Perplexity, accusing the startup of concealing its Comet agent, which can purchase products on behalf of users. 
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said the company expects "over time, to partner with third-party agents," but that any partnerships will require the right "value exchange" between agents and retailers... 
For now, agents remain a niche tool for shopping, with agentic purchases making up just 0.4% of global e-commerce transactions and 0.2% of value, according to Bain & Co. research published earlier this month... But retailers may not be able to ignore them forever. Roughly a quarter of Muse's 10 million users are shopping online via an AI agent with an average spend of $200 per order, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said in October. 
The article notes bots often "get stumped by login requirements at checkout. In some cases, the agents may require human intervention to bypass a Captcha test and continue browsing... 

"A Visa study published earlier this month instructed 22 models from 12 AI labs to carry out a range of shopping tasks, such as buying a TV, a laptop and a hair appliance. The agents failed about 43% of test runs, and in more than half of those failed runs, an agent purchased a product "that did not meet the customer's identified requirements," according to the study..."





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Chinese Data Center Tied to Alice Huang Found Using Nvidia's Powerful AI Chips
description:
Friday Nvidia's stock showed a 30.95% drop over the last month, and a 37% drop from its October 2nd high of $239.24. But it managed a 4.83% gain for the week — after some bad news hit Friday morning... 

A Chinese data center with ties to Alice Huang (the suspected Chinese spy-agency asset) "has installed hardware with Nvidia's powerful Blackwell AI chips," writes Gizmodo, citing a Friday morning report from Bloomberg. Those chips are "among Nvidia's most powerful products," writes Bloomberg, and their presence was confirmed by "a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November," (offering the hardware as collateral for a $14 million loan, according to bank filings seen by Bloomberg News). 
A second Chinese company (this one controlled by a Tokyo-based parent company) also described a server with Nvidia's advanced Blackwell chips in documents for a similar loan in late 2025 from, Bloomberg reports:

The submissions reveal for the first time that Nvidia's Blackwell processors found their way into a Chinese data center that has ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. [Alice Huang has ties to "a number of companies" that invested in the second company, and its president is her husband Kang Wei.] 

These processors were until recently Nvidia's most powerful data center products, and they've always been illegal to ship to China without a US license. President Donald Trump has explicitly said he doesn't want these chips — which OpenAI and Anthropic PBC use to train their most cutting-edge models — going to the Asian country, at least for now. Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, meanwhile, once claimed they were too big to smuggle: a standard two-meter-tall GB300 NVL72 server rack, which contains 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, can weigh more than 1,500 kilograms (3,300 pounds) and is about the size of a gigantic fridge... 

Shanghai Shuoyao — the company that procured the GB300 rack and offered it as collateral — is active at the data center linked to Alice Huang and also has significant overlap with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is under US investigation over concerns that it smuggled Nvidia chips to China, Bloomberg has reported. Shanghai Shuoyao, which hasn't responded to Bloomberg queries over the past year, confirmed this month in a rare public statement that it is one of Megaspeed's service providers, describing the partnership as "limited to ordinary commercial cooperation." 

Megaspeed, meanwhile, used a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project in 2024 to describe its largest data center to investors, dubbing the site a "specific area" facility in an unnamed country... The parameters they've outlined in construction plans reviewed by Bloomberg — specifically, the total processing power as compared to the energy input — would be extremely difficult to satisfy with chips from Chinese companies such as Huawei Technologies Co.
 
Bloomberg says Nvidia "has not answered repeated queries," though they add that Nvida "for years insisted that there was no black market for its products." 

The article also notes that Megaspeed (where Alice Huang worked) "won a coveted stamp of approval from Nvidia within four days of its creation" in 2023, and went on to become Nvidia's largest customer in Southeast Asia.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Mozilla Thanks Users For New Features in Firefox 161: Site-Specific VPN and Keyboard Shortcuts
description:
Firefox 161 (released Tuesday) promises "A better Firefox, thanks to you. All of these improvements began with a community request." In a Thanksgiving-themed message, they wrote "Here's to the passionate people who keep us moving forward."




Choose which sites always open with VPN. Our free built-in VPN just got one of its most requested upgrades. Pick sites where the VPN always turns on, and sites where it stays off because they work better without it. Bonus: VPN data is unlimited through January. Use it as much as you like until then... 
Set your own shortcuts . Create keyboard shortcuts for what you use most, like opening tabs, saving pages or closing windows. Type "about:keyboard" in the address bar. 

See images appear as they load. Firefox now supports JPEG XL, an image format that lets you see a preview of the full image before it downloads. 

Neowin notes Firefox is also committing to its redesign:

Mozilla has been trying to win over users from Chromium-based browsers, hoping they pick up Firefox. To do so, aside from still supporting uBlock Origin, the firm made a big design shift this year by introducing Nova, so that users on the other side can feel they are familiar with it, as it brings the more common, modern rounded corner design philosophy, which Google's Chrome has been using for quite a while... However, as is usually the case, not everyone has been on-board with Nova and they are completely fine to feel that way; Mozilla also understands this which is why it offered a way to opt-out of it by tweaking a configuration setting via about:config. However, this week the firm announced that it is going to take that option away. 



In a post on its official Mozilla Connect forum, which was shared with us by Neowin forum member ecmram, the Firefox team confirmed that it will remove the config toggle preference for reverting to the old design next month in December. The company says that the rollout of Nova is now complete, and it wants to lock the preference to ensure that Firefox performs as intended and to prevent unexpected browser behavior. As such, anyone who has previously used the browser.nova.enabled preference to disable the redesign will automatically get Nova starting next month, thus wiping the official way to return to the previous UI once the change takes effect. 


On the positive side, Mozilla is not entirely ignoring feedback from users who are unhappy with the redesign. The company says it has introduced several changes based on community feedback, including a new set of Classic Themes with the latest version 161, that offer flat colors without gradients. These can be found under about:addons, and one of them even mimics the older Proton design with a gray appearance. There is a new Fire toolbar button too that clears history with a single-click.






Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Nvidia Seeded Pirated Books and Shared Them With Adobe, Authors Allege
description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TorrentFreak: Several book authors have filed (PDF) an amended complaint accusing Nvidia of seeding pirated books via BitTorrent, after downloading them from shadow libraries including Anna's Archive and LibGen. [...] These tools can download files via BitTorrent, and the authors and Nvidia both agree that whether they also upload data to others depends on the settings used. According to the authors, Nvidia didn't prevent seeding altogether. "When Nvidia ran the BitTorrent client, Nvidia uploaded pieces of pirated book files to third parties during the downloading process (i.e., before the download was complete). Nvidia also 'seeded' pirated books (i.e., made available and uploaded parts of a completely downloaded file). While Nvidia took some steps to limit seeding, it did not prevent seeding altogether," the complaint reads.
 
The authors say they found out in June, when Nvidia handed over the code it used for torrenting. Based on that code, they were "able to determine that Nvidia did not disable uploading," the authors told the court. The complaint states that the authors' own books were among those Nvidia downloaded. However, the claim that they were also uploaded to others is made "on information and belief," which essentially means the authors don't have direct knowledge of it. In addition to the seeding claims, the authors also allege that Nvidia shared the pirated books with business partners, including Adobe, through a "PDF Extraction Project" involving 250 million pages. These pages were acquired in part from shadow libraries such as Anna's Archive and LibGen.
 
According to the complaint, Nvidia shared its pirated books with Adobe because it wanted to "get tokens out of PDFs to create differentiated models" and "include PDF extraction into our NeMo pipeline so that customers can leverage their PDF content." In return, the complaint says, Adobe committed to using Nvidia's language models in some of its products. That made the deal a big opportunity for Nvidia, with its NeMo AI models potentially "powering every one of Adobe PDFs," the authors write. Adobe wasn't the only partner. The complaint also mentions partnerships with Cohere and Imbue that involved sharing Nvidia's base training data and offering books acquired from shadow libraries. The authors believe their own books were shared with all three companies, but this is alleged on information and belief. With these allegations, the amended complaint now accuses Nvidia of distributing the books itself and of helping others to infringe, which falls under its existing direct and contributory infringement claims.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: James T. Russell, Physicist Who Pioneered CD and DVD Technology, Dies At 95
description:
James T. Russell, the American physicist whose pioneering digital-to-optical recording and playback system laid the foundation for CD, DVD and Blu-ray technology, has died at the age of 95. "Russell never became a household name, but the technology he developed, later licensed by Sony and Phillips, would transform everything from the way people listen to music to the way data is stored," reports The Daily Chronicle. From the report: In a career spanning almost his entire life, Russell earned more than 70 patents, but his biggest breakthrough was the invention of the first digital-to-optical recording and playback system in the 1960s and early 1970s, a system that brought crystal clear audio and film to the masses. [...] It was in Richland that Russell started exploring how to create cleaner recordings of music. Popping and hissing often accompanied the music of vinyl records, from the analog sound of a needle scraping against microgrooves, and Russell thought he could do something about it. He crunched the numbers before bringing an invention report to Battelle: What if a light beam could read a digital record?
 
"It isn't clear what the problem was," Russell recalled in a Seattle Times interview in 2004. "I think there was some feeling amongst the moneybags that it probably wouldn't work, (or) if it did work there's no advantage, no value in optical records. What would you use it for, and would people want it and, anyway, if it was any good, IBM would have already invented it." While his idea faced skepticism early on, the company gave him some money to experiment. Russell invented an early method to store audio digitally and play it back to produce a flawless sound. He also created a way to store digital information densely.
 
Other primitive, analog laser disk technology had been developed in the 1950s by engineer David Paul Gregg. Russell's earliest patents in the field were issued in the mid-1960s, with a working prototype finished by the 1970s, using a laser to read binary data on a compact disc, or CD. The patent for Russell's invention passed from company to company, bringing him from Richland to Salt Lake City, then to Toronto. His development of the first digital-to-optical recording and playback system became foundational to CD-ROM, DVD and Blu-ray technology. Russell didn't earn royalties, never made a fortune, and was rarely credited for his work.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Scientists Used Seabirds To Track Hidden Ships
description:
Scientists equipped seabirds with audio recorders and GPS trackers to detect fishing vessels that were not broadcasting their locations through the Automatic Identification System (AIS), according to a new study published in Science Advances. They found that unseen vessels accounted for about 32% of vessel-related audio detections in the North Atlantic and 12% in the Mediterranean. "The one petrel in the study interacted with vessels in the South Pacific, but its geolocation device was damaged, so it was not possible to calculate how many ships it encountered had their trackers off," adds 404 Media. From the report: Many vessels are required to continuously signal their location using the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which openly broadcasts a ship's location, similar to flight tracking. But AIS can be disabled for legitimate reasons -- such as evading pirates -- or with more nefarious motivations, such as concealment of illegal fishing activities. The new study was not designed to interrogate why any particular vessel switched off its AIS tracker. However, the discovery that seabirds are regularly interacting with unseen ships can shed light on broader efforts to monitor commercial fisheries, while also revealing new insights about seabird behavior, especially their risk of becoming "bycatch" when they are fatally trapped in fishing gear.
 
Unseen vessel activity "is concerning, or at least important, regardless of whether it's legal or illegal," said Jonathan Rutter, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Oxford who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. He added that the recordings were not intended to be used for law-enforcement or surveillance, but that this line of research could become a "powerful tool for improving risk assessment" by recording seabird-vessel interactions that would otherwise be off the map.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: A Man In Denver Has Been Trapping Waymos
description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: A bearded man with a brown ponytail has been on the hunt for Waymos in Denver, trapping the self-driving taxis so they can't pull away (source paywalled; alternative source) and hurling cartons of eggs at them, the police and company officials said. There have been at least 30 episodes of the egg attacks, according to Waymo, and a company investigator reported seven of them to the Denver police, all believed to be linked to the same man, according to a police report filed last month. [...] The man, who remains unidentified, stopped in front of the Waymo vans and S.U.V.s circulating in and around downtown Denver, according to the police report. Then, he removed orange cones from his car's trunk and placed them around the vehicles "to prevent the Waymo vehicle from moving," the report said. In some instances, the man threw eggs "while seated inside his vehicle" and at other times he "throws eggs at the Waymo vehicle after exiting his vehicle," the report said. The man then fled in a silver Toyota Corolla, which according to the report is part of a fleet of vehicles "able to be leased for Lyft drivers." Waymo said they had to temporarily pull the egged vehicles from service and spend about $2,000 on cleaning, though no permanent damage was reported.
 
Denver prosecutors declined to file criminal charges, deeming the case a civil matter, but are continuing to collect evidence and explore legal options to stop the behavior. The driver remains unidentified.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: NYT Warns Photographers Not To Update Photoshop Over AI Features
description:
The New York Times is instructing freelance photographers not to use Adobe Photoshop 2027 (version 28.0.0 and subsequent updates), warning that its new AI features operate "in ways that may not be apparent to users" and "can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated." The Verge reports: It's not always clear which tools in Adobe's apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers' trust.
 
Last year, the Times said that it does not "retouch or digitally manipulate" photos but may "make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image." In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: S&P Warns Nvidia's Board May Be Compromised
description:
S&P Global Ratings has placed Nvidia's AA credit rating on downgrade watch, warning that Jensen Huang's departure and subsequent reinstatement as CEO exposed weaknesses in the company's corporate governance and board oversight. "We believe the long tenure of certain board members may have compromised their independence. The company's corporate governance practices may also not have kept pace with Nvidia's rapid growth and its role as a critical global technology enabler," the ratings agency said. Reuters reports: Nvidia currently has an 'AA' rating from S&P, which indicates a very strong capacity to meet financial commitments. The highest rating is 'AAA'. The agency said it could downgrade Nvidia within the next 90 days, but expects any potential downgrade to be limited to one notch, unless investigations and other disclosures harm the company's reputation or future business prospects. Meanwhile, Moody's said on Wednesday that bringing back Huang eases near-term uncertainty around Nvidia's business execution and eliminates execution risk associated with appointing a new leader for the chipmaker. The agency said Nvidia's Aa1 rating and stable outlook remain unaffected, but added that governance and regulatory uncertainty persists.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.
